diabetes_type2.name: Type 2 Diabetes
diabetes_type2.description: A chronic metabolic disorder where the body either does not produce enough insulin or does not use it effectively, causing blood sugar to remain persistently elevated. One of the fastest-growing conditions in Uganda — estimates suggest up to 8% of Kampala residents may have it, most undiagnosed.
diabetes_type2.body_mechanism: Insulin is produced by the pancreas to help cells absorb glucose from the blood. In Type 2 diabetes, cells become resistant to insulin signals — they stop responding properly. The pancreas works harder and harder to produce more insulin, eventually becoming exhausted. Blood glucose stays high and damages blood vessels, nerves, kidneys, and eyes over years. The damage is silent until it is advanced, which is why early detection is critical.
diabetes_type2.epidemiology_uganda: Estimated 8% of Kampala adults have type 2 diabetes. Uganda has seen a rapid rise in NCD burden alongside infectious diseases, creating a 'double burden'. Most cases remain undiagnosed due to lack of screening.

immediate: See a doctor or nurse TODAY for a blood glucose test — this is the only way to know
Avoid sugary drinks, white bread, and processed foods until you are tested
If you feel dizzy, confused, or extremely thirsty — drink water (not juice) immediately
Do not self-medicate with traditional herbs without medical guidance — they can interact with proper treatment
If you are already diagnosed and feel very unwell, go to hospital — could be diabetic emergency
short_term: Get your blood glucose tested — fasting glucose test or HbA1c are the standard
If diagnosed, start the medication exactly as prescribed — never stop without doctor advice
Reduce sugar, refined carbohydrates (white rice, posho, bread), and sugary drinks drastically
Begin walking 30 minutes daily — exercise lowers blood glucose more effectively than many drugs
Check your feet daily for cuts, sores, or numbness — diabetic foot problems can escalate fast
long_term: Eat smaller portions of staple foods — maize, rice, cassava all raise blood glucose significantly
Increase vegetables, legumes (beans, lentils), and lean protein at every meal
Get HbA1c checked every 3 months — shows average blood glucose over 3 months
Have eyes, kidneys (urine test), and feet checked at least once a year
Maintain healthy weight — every kilogram lost significantly improves glucose control
Quit smoking if applicable — tobacco causes the very vascular damage diabetes worsens

see_doctor_if: Extremely high thirst, frequent urination, and rapid unexplained weight loss — possible new diabetes
Confusion, extreme weakness, rapid breathing — could be diabetic ketoacidosis (emergency)
Any foot wound that is not healing normally within 1 week
Sudden vision changes
Blood glucose reading above 20 mmol/L or below 3.5 mmol/L on a glucometer
diabetes_type2.local_context: Diabetes is dramatically rising in Uganda as diets shift toward processed foods and sugar-sweetened drinks. The typical Ugandan diet — posho, matoke, white rice — is high in refined carbohydrates that spike blood glucose. Many Ugandans with diabetes have no symptoms for years until serious complications arise. If you are over 35, overweight, or have family history — test today.
home_remedies: Bitter leaf (Vernonia amygdalina / Omujjajjali) — traditional remedy with evidence of mild glucose-lowering effect. Use as a supplement, not replacement for medication
Moringa leaves — emerging evidence of blood glucose benefit. Can be dried and added to food
Walking 30–45 minutes daily — the most powerful blood glucose tool available without a prescription
Reduce sugar: replace sodas with water, reduce added sugar in tea/coffee
Fenugreek seeds soaked overnight — traditional remedy with some evidence of glucose benefit

tuberculosis.name: Tuberculosis (TB)
tuberculosis.description: A serious bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs but capable of affecting any organ. Africa accounts for 25% of global TB cases and 42% of TB deaths. Uganda is classified as a high-burden TB country. TB is curable with the correct antibiotic course.
tuberculosis.body_mechanism: TB bacteria are inhaled through the air from an infected person who coughs, sneezes, or talks. The bacteria settle in the lungs where the immune system walls them off in granulomas. In most people they stay dormant (latent TB). When the immune system weakens — from HIV, malnutrition, stress, or age — the bacteria reactivate, destroy lung tissue, and produce the classic symptoms. The characteristic cough lasting weeks produces mucus and sometimes blood as the bacteria erode the airways.
tuberculosis.epidemiology_uganda: Uganda is a high TB-burden country. TB is the leading infectious cause of death globally. HIV co-infection dramatically increases TB risk — someone with HIV is 18x more likely to develop active TB. TB and HIV together cause significant mortality in Uganda.

immediate: Cover your mouth and nose when coughing — TB is airborne and you may be contagious
Go to your nearest health centre for a sputum test and chest X-ray — free at government facilities
Tell the health worker how long you have been coughing — this is critical diagnostic information
Do not share cups, plates, or close spaces with others until you have been assessed
If you have HIV and develop a cough — go to hospital today. TB + HIV is a medical emergency
short_term: If TB is confirmed, start treatment immediately — treatment is FREE at all government health facilities in Uganda
Take ALL the medication EVERY DAY for the FULL course (typically 6 months) — stopping early causes drug-resistant TB
Register with the Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) programme if your health centre offers it
Eat nutritious food — TB is worsened by malnutrition. Protein (beans, eggs, meat), vitamins, calories
Open your living space — fresh air and sunlight kill TB bacteria
long_term: Complete the full 6-month treatment — even if you feel better after 2 months
Test all household contacts for TB — especially children and those with HIV
Get tested for HIV if you haven't — TB and HIV require coordinated treatment
Improve nutrition, sleep, and reduce alcohol — these strengthen immunity against TB reactivation
Regular ventilation of your home — TB spreads in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces

see_doctor_if: Cough lasting more than 2 weeks — especially with fever and weight loss
Coughing up blood or blood-stained mucus at any point
Night sweats that soak your clothing — classic TB symptom
Unexplained weight loss of more than 2kg without dieting
Chest pain with coughing
Any of these symptoms if you have HIV — urgent
tuberculosis.local_context: TB is common across Uganda, especially in crowded urban areas like Kampala slums, and in people living with HIV. Government health facilities provide free TB testing and treatment. There is no need to pay for TB care in Uganda. The 'three Cs' of TB concern: Cough over 2 weeks, Constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), Contact with a TB patient.
home_remedies: TB MUST be treated with antibiotics — there are no effective herbal substitutes
Nutritious diet is essential: protein (beans, groundnuts, eggs, meat), vitamin C (fruits), zinc
Fresh air and sunlight in the home — these naturally reduce bacterial load in the environment
Rest adequately — your immune system does its best work when you sleep well
Avoid alcohol completely during treatment — it interferes with TB medications and damages the liver

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.description: A serious lung infection causing the air sacs (alveoli) to fill with fluid or pus, making breathing painful and difficult. Pneumonia is the leading cause of death in children under 5 in Uganda and a top killer across all ages. It can be bacterial, viral, or fungal and always requires prompt medical attention.
pneumonia.body_mechanism: Bacteria or viruses infect the alveoli — the tiny sacs where oxygen transfers to blood. The immune response floods these sacs with fluid and white blood cells, making gas exchange very difficult. This is why pneumonia causes breathlessness, low oxygen, and the characteristic productive cough as the body tries to clear the infected fluid. Without treatment, oxygen levels fall and organs begin to fail.

immediate: GO TO A HEALTH FACILITY OR HOSPITAL TODAY — pneumonia is life-threatening if untreated
Sit upright — this position makes breathing easier than lying down
Take paracetamol for fever — do not take ibuprofen if breathing is already difficult
Drink plenty of water to stay hydrated
If breathing is very difficult or lips are turning blue — this is an EMERGENCY. Go now.
short_term: Take the full course of antibiotics prescribed — even if you feel better after 3 days
Rest completely — pneumonia is serious and requires genuine rest to recover
Prop yourself upright when sleeping — use extra pillows
Monitor your breathing rate — if it is increasing, return to hospital
Eat small nutritious meals to maintain immune strength
long_term: Complete full antibiotic course — incomplete treatment leads to antibiotic resistance
Avoid smoking completely — smoking destroys the lung defences that prevent pneumonia
Vaccinate children against pneumococcal pneumonia — this vaccine is available in Uganda
Improve indoor air quality — cooking smoke is a major risk factor for pneumonia in Uganda
If HIV positive, discuss preventive treatment options with your doctor

see_doctor_if: ANY case of suspected pneumonia — this condition always needs medical assessment
Rapid breathing (more than 30 breaths per minute in adults)
Blue lips or fingernails — go to hospital immediately
Confusion or difficulty staying awake
Chest pain that is severe or worsening
Child under 5 with fever and fast breathing — go to hospital NOW
pneumonia.local_context: Pneumonia kills more children in Uganda than any other disease. Indoor cooking smoke, malnutrition, and HIV co-infection dramatically increase the risk. Free antibiotics for pneumonia are available at government health facilities. Distinguish from TB: pneumonia comes on more suddenly, while TB develops over weeks. Both need immediate medical assessment.
home_remedies: Pneumonia REQUIRES antibiotics — home remedies alone are not sufficient
Steam inhalation helps loosen mucus and ease breathing while getting medical care
Stay upright — gravity helps clear fluid from the lower lungs
Honey and warm water — soothes the throat and airway (not for children under 1)
Adequate hydration — helps thin the mucus and supports immune function

diabetes_emergency.name: Diabetic Emergency
diabetes_emergency.description: A life-threatening condition in a person with diabetes where blood glucose is dangerously high (hyperglycaemia/DKA) or dangerously low (hypoglycaemia). Both require immediate action.
diabetes_emergency.body_mechanism: In hypoglycaemia, blood glucose falls so low that the brain — which runs entirely on glucose — starts to shut down, causing confusion, trembling, and unconsciousness. In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), no insulin means cells starve. The body breaks down fat for energy, producing toxic ketones that acidify the blood, causing vomiting, rapid breathing, and coma.

immediate: If conscious and hypoglycaemia suspected (shaky, sweating, confused): give sugar NOW — 3 glucose tablets, or 150ml fruit juice, or 3 teaspoons of sugar dissolved in water
If improving after 15 minutes, give a carbohydrate snack (bread, banana)
If not improving or unconscious: GO TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY — do not try to give food/drink to an unconscious person
If DKA suspected (fruity breath, rapid breathing, vomiting): GO TO HOSPITAL NOW
Never leave a diabetic person who is confused or semi-conscious alone
short_term: After any diabetic emergency, review medication and diet with a doctor
Identify what triggered the episode — skipped meal, too much insulin, illness, exercise
Always carry fast-acting sugar (glucose tablets or hard sweets) if on insulin or sulfonylureas
Family members should know how to recognise and respond to hypoglycaemia
long_term: Never skip meals if on insulin or certain tablets
Monitor glucose more frequently during illness or unusual physical activity
Wear a medical alert bracelet or keep a card in your wallet noting diabetic status
Teach family members the signs of low blood glucose and what to do

see_doctor_if: ANY diabetic who is confused, unconscious, or cannot be roused — EMERGENCY NOW
Rapid or laboured breathing with vomiting in a known diabetic
Blood glucose reading below 3.5 mmol/L that does not respond to sugar intake
Blood glucose above 25 mmol/L with symptoms
diabetes_emergency.local_context: Diabetic emergencies are increasingly common in Uganda as diabetes prevalence rises. Many people do not realise they have diabetes until they present in crisis. Hypoglycaemia is common in diabetics who skip meals — very common in Uganda where meal timing is irregular.
home_remedies: Immediate: Give sugar — glucose tablets, fruit juice, sugar water
Wait 15 minutes and re-assess
If no improvement: hospital immediately
Prevention: never skip meals, carry quick sugar, take medication at consistent times

sickle_cell.name: Sickle Cell Disease / Crisis
sickle_cell.description: A genetic blood disorder common in sub-Saharan Africa where red blood cells become abnormally shaped (sickle-shaped) and block blood vessels. Uganda has one of the highest sickle cell prevalence rates in the world — about 20,000 children are born with it annually in Uganda.
sickle_cell.body_mechanism: Normal red blood cells are round and flexible, flowing easily through vessels. Sickle cells are rigid and crescent-shaped. They clump together and block small blood vessels, cutting off oxygen to tissues and organs. This causes the severe pain of a 'crisis' — the body's tissues literally starving for oxygen. The abnormal cells also break down quickly, causing chronic anaemia.
sickle_cell.epidemiology_uganda: Uganda has extremely high sickle cell prevalence — roughly 1 in 25 Ugandans carries the sickle cell trait. About 15,000-20,000 children are born with sickle cell disease annually. It is most prevalent in the western, northern, and eastern regions.

immediate: Drink large amounts of water — dehydration is the #1 trigger of sickle cell crisis
Take your prescribed pain medication (paracetamol or stronger as prescribed) immediately
Apply warm compresses to the area of pain — warmth relieves vascular spasm
Rest completely — do not push through a crisis
Go to hospital if the pain is severe, if fever develops, or if breathing is affected
short_term: Stay hydrated at all times — carry water everywhere
Take prescribed hydroxyurea or folic acid exactly as directed
Avoid cold temperatures — cold triggers vessel constriction and crisis
Avoid high altitude and strenuous exercise without preparation
Get infections treated promptly — infections are a major crisis trigger
long_term: Attend the sickle cell clinic regularly — monitoring prevents complications
Take folic acid daily — helps produce healthy red blood cells
Vaccinate against pneumococcal pneumonia and influenza — critical with sickle cell
Drink 8-10 glasses of water daily, every single day — non-negotiable
Genetic counselling if planning a family — carrier testing for partner is important

see_doctor_if: Severe pain crisis not responding to home pain management within 2 hours
Fever above 38.5°C — sickle cell patients are at high risk of serious infections
Breathing difficulty or chest pain during a crisis — could be acute chest syndrome
Stroke symptoms: sudden weakness, vision loss, difficulty speaking
Severe headache or neck stiffness
Priapism (painful prolonged erection in men) — urological emergency
sickle_cell.local_context: Uganda has one of the highest sickle cell burdens in the world. Many families do not know a child has sickle cell disease until a crisis occurs. Government hospitals provide free sickle cell treatment under the National Sickle Cell Programme. Children with sickle cell should be identified early and enrolled in the programme.
home_remedies: Water, water, water — the most powerful sickle cell prevention tool
Warm compresses on painful areas
Paracetamol for mild-to-moderate pain (avoid ibuprofen if kidneys are affected)
Rest and warmth during a crisis
Folic acid daily — helps build healthy red blood cells, available cheaply in Uganda

malnutrition.name: Malnutrition / Nutritional Deficiency
malnutrition.description: A condition resulting from inadequate intake or absorption of essential nutrients — protein, calories, vitamins, or minerals. Very common in Uganda, especially in children, pregnant women, and people with chronic illness. Malnutrition worsens every other health condition and is a major cause of child mortality.
malnutrition.body_mechanism: The body requires a constant supply of macro and micronutrients to maintain immune function, growth, wound healing, brain function, and energy. When intake falls short, the body breaks down its own muscle and fat for energy. The immune system weakens, making infections more severe. In children, brain development is permanently impaired by early malnutrition. Specific deficiencies cause specific diseases: iron deficiency causes anaemia, vitamin A deficiency causes blindness, iodine deficiency causes goitre.

immediate: If a child appears severely wasted (very thin, swollen feet, apathetic) — go to health facility TODAY
Eat protein at every meal: beans, lentils, groundnuts, eggs, fish, meat
Include colourful vegetables and fruits daily — these provide essential vitamins
If breastfeeding: continue breastfeeding while improving your own diet
ORS (oral rehydration salts) if dehydration is suspected alongside malnutrition
short_term: Prioritise protein intake at every meal — malnutrition is primarily a protein energy problem
Include iron-rich foods: dark leafy greens (sukuma wiki), beans, liver, red meat
Include vitamin C-rich foods with iron-rich meals — dramatically improves iron absorption
If child has malnutrition, seek referral to therapeutic feeding programme — available free at health centres
Deworm every 6 months — worms significantly worsen malnutrition by stealing nutrients
long_term: Grow and eat diverse foods — kitchen gardens provide year-round vegetable access
Ensure children receive all vaccinations — vaccinated children absorb food better
Practice exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, then introduce diverse solid foods
Deworm all children regularly — available free at government health facilities
Improve hygiene — infections drain nutrients and reduce appetite

see_doctor_if: Child with visible wasting — thin limbs, prominent ribs, apathetic
Swollen feet or legs in a child (kwashiorkor) — always a medical emergency
Child not eating for more than 24 hours
Pregnant woman losing weight
Any adult losing weight unexpectedly without trying
malnutrition.local_context: Malnutrition in Uganda often coexists with food insecurity, especially in northern and eastern regions. Even in Kampala, diets high in posho, matoke, and rice with minimal protein and vegetables are common. Iron deficiency anaemia affects over 50% of children under 5 in Uganda. Vitamin A supplementation programmes exist — ensure your child receives them at health centres.
home_remedies: Increase protein: beans, groundnuts, silver fish (mukene), eggs, soya
Dark leafy greens: sukuma wiki, malakwang, nakati — eaten with vitamin C sources
Porridge enriched with groundnut paste — high calorie and protein for young children
Moringa powder — extremely nutrient-dense, add to porridge or sauces
Avoid giving children tea — it blocks iron absorption. Give water or milk instead

conjunctivitis.name: Conjunctivitis (Pink Eye)
conjunctivitis.description: Inflammation of the conjunctiva — the clear membrane covering the white of the eye and inner eyelid. Extremely common in Uganda, particularly in children. Can be bacterial (yellow/green discharge), viral (watery, more contagious), or allergic (itchy, both eyes).
conjunctivitis.body_mechanism: The conjunctiva is exposed to the environment constantly. When bacteria, viruses, or allergens irritate it, the immune system responds with inflammation — causing redness, discharge, and the sensation of grit in the eye. Bacterial conjunctivitis produces thick discharge that may seal the eye shut on waking. Viral spreads very easily through hand-to-eye contact. Allergic is not contagious but recurs with allergen exposure.

immediate: Clean the eye gently with clean cotton wool soaked in clean warm water — remove discharge
Do not rub the eye — this spreads the infection and worsens irritation
Wash hands thoroughly before and after touching your eyes
If bacterial (thick yellow/green discharge): see a health worker for antibiotic eye drops
Keep the infected eye covered or away from others — viral conjunctivitis is highly contagious
short_term: Apply antibiotic eye drops if prescribed — 4-6 times daily for 5-7 days
Do not share towels, pillows, or eye makeup with others
Change pillowcases daily while infected
Wear sunglasses if light sensitivity is present
For allergic conjunctivitis: avoid the trigger, cold compresses help with itching
long_term: Practice hand hygiene — the main way conjunctivitis spreads
Do not share personal items that touch the face
For recurring allergic conjunctivitis: identify and avoid triggers (dust, pollen, cosmetics)
Keep your home well-ventilated and reduce dust in sleeping areas

see_doctor_if: Vision changes or blurred vision with eye redness
Severe eye pain — not just discomfort
No improvement after 3 days of treatment
Redness in a newborn — always needs urgent assessment
Sensitivity to light with headache — could indicate uveitis or meningitis
conjunctivitis.local_context: Conjunctivitis is extremely common in Uganda, especially in schools and crowded communities. Viral conjunctivitis spreads rapidly in dry, dusty conditions. Antibiotic eye drops are available at most pharmacies and government health centres. Many cases in Uganda are bacterial and respond well to chloramphenicol eye drops.
home_remedies: Warm clean water compresses — clean the discharge and soothe irritation
Cold compresses for allergic conjunctivitis — reduces itching and swelling
Clean hands before touching eyes — always
Honey dissolved in warm water as eye wash — traditional remedy with some antibacterial evidence (use very dilute solution)
Cucumber slices on closed eyes — cooling and soothing for allergic types

diarrhoea_acute.name: Acute Diarrhoea / Gastroenteritis
diarrhoea_acute.description: Sudden onset of loose or watery stools, often with stomach cramps, nausea, and vomiting. Usually caused by contaminated food or water (bacteria, viruses, or parasites). The leading cause of child mortality in Uganda is dehydration from diarrhoea. Most cases resolve in 3-7 days with proper hydration.
diarrhoea_acute.body_mechanism: Pathogens enter the gut and irritate or invade the intestinal lining. The gut responds by secreting large amounts of fluid to flush out the infection — this produces watery stools. The body loses enormous amounts of water, salts, and electrolytes. Dehydration sets in rapidly, especially in children and the elderly. The electrolyte losses (particularly sodium and potassium) affect heart and muscle function — this is what makes diarrhoea potentially fatal.

immediate: Start ORS (Oral Rehydration Salts) immediately — available at every pharmacy and health centre in Uganda
Drink ORS in small sips frequently — not large amounts at once if vomiting
If no ORS available: mix 1 litre clean water + 6 level teaspoons sugar + 0.5 teaspoon salt
For a child: give ORS after every loose stool — about 100-200ml per stool
CONTINUE FEEDING — do not stop eating or breast milk. Food helps recovery
short_term: Drink more fluids than usual to replace losses — water, ORS, coconut water, clear broth
Eat soft, easily digestible foods: rice, banana, boiled potato, plain bread
Avoid dairy, fatty foods, and raw vegetables until fully recovered
Wash hands thoroughly with soap before eating and after toilet — prevent spreading
If symptoms worsen or do not improve in 3 days, see a doctor
long_term: Drink only treated, boiled, or bottled water
Wash hands with soap before cooking and eating, after toilet
Store food properly — cooked food should not sit at room temperature for more than 2 hours
Keep food covered from flies
Ensure all children receive rotavirus vaccination — prevents the most common severe diarrhoea

see_doctor_if: Blood or pus in stools — could indicate dysentery or cholera
Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, dry mouth, no urine for 8 hours, extreme weakness
Diarrhoea in a child under 1 year — always needs medical assessment
More than 10 loose stools per day
High fever with diarrhoea
Symptoms not improving after 3 days
diarrhoea_acute.local_context: Diarrhoeal disease is the second leading cause of child death in Uganda after malaria. Contaminated water and poor sanitation are the primary causes. ORS is the single most life-saving treatment — available free at government health centres. Many deaths occur because families do not know to use ORS or wait too long to seek care. Give ORS first, then seek help.
home_remedies: ORS — the most important treatment. Make at home if needed: 1L water + 6tsp sugar + 0.5tsp salt
Banana — contains potassium lost through diarrhoea, BRAT diet staple
Plain boiled rice — easily digestible, provides energy without stressing gut
Coconut water — naturally contains electrolytes, good rehydration fluid
Ginger tea — anti-nausea and anti-spasmodic properties. Slice fresh ginger, boil 10 minutes

hypertensive_crisis.name: Hypertensive Crisis
hypertensive_crisis.description: A medical emergency where blood pressure rises to extremely dangerous levels (typically above 180/120 mmHg), potentially causing immediate organ damage — stroke, heart attack, kidney failure, or vision loss.
hypertensive_crisis.body_mechanism: At extremely high pressures, blood vessel walls are stressed beyond their limits. Vessels can rupture (causing stroke or bleeding in the eye), the heart strains severely (causing chest pain or heart attack), and the kidneys begin to fail under the pressure load. Every minute of extremely high blood pressure increases the risk of permanent, irreversible damage.

immediate: STOP all activity — sit or lie down quietly immediately
If you have prescribed blood pressure medication: take it NOW
Go to hospital — do not drive yourself. Call for help or have someone drive you
Avoid stimulants: no coffee, tea, cigarettes, or physical exertion
Do not take extra blood pressure medication beyond your prescribed dose without guidance
short_term: Hospital treatment required — IV medications and monitoring
Review all medications with doctor
Identify and address precipitating cause
long_term: Never miss blood pressure medication
Regular monitoring
Lifestyle modification

see_doctor_if: ANY reading above 180/120 mmHg — go to hospital immediately
Severe headache with vision changes
Chest pain with high blood pressure
Confusion or difficulty speaking with high blood pressure
hypertensive_crisis.local_context: Hypertensive crisis is increasingly seen in Uganda as undiagnosed and uncontrolled hypertension is very common. Many people stop medication when they feel better — this is extremely dangerous and commonly leads to crisis.
home_remedies: This is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY — home remedies are not appropriate
Take your prescribed medication if you have it
Sit quietly and get to hospital as fast as possible
Call for someone to help you — do not drive

anaemia.name: Anaemia (Iron Deficiency)
anaemia.description: A condition where the blood lacks enough healthy red blood cells or haemoglobin to carry adequate oxygen throughout the body. Iron deficiency is the most common cause. Over 50% of Ugandan children under 5 and over 40% of pregnant women in Uganda have anaemia.
anaemia.body_mechanism: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin — a protein that requires iron. When iron is depleted (through poor diet, blood loss, worm infestation, or malaria), haemoglobin production falls, cells shrink, and the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity drops. Every tissue in the body receives less oxygen — causing the fatigue, pallor, breathlessness, and poor concentration characteristic of anaemia.
anaemia.epidemiology_uganda: Anaemia affects over 50% of children under 5 and 40% of pregnant women in Uganda. Major causes: iron-poor diet, malaria (destroys red blood cells), intestinal worms (steal iron), and repeated pregnancies. Sickle cell disease also causes chronic haemolytic anaemia.

immediate: Get a blood test at your nearest health centre — haemoglobin measurement diagnoses anaemia
Start eating iron-rich foods at every meal: dark leafy greens, beans, liver, fish, meat
Eat iron-rich foods WITH vitamin C — dramatically improves iron absorption
Stop drinking tea with meals — tea blocks iron absorption significantly
If pregnant with anaemia: see a midwife or doctor today — it affects the baby
short_term: Take iron supplements as prescribed — they cause black stools which is normal
Deworm — intestinal worms steal iron. Free deworming at government health centres
Test for malaria if you have been ill recently — malaria destroys red blood cells
Eat vitamin C with iron-rich foods: tomatoes, oranges, pawpaw with beans
Avoid drinking tea or coffee within an hour of meals while treating anaemia
long_term: Maintain iron-rich diet long-term: beans, dark leafy greens, fish, liver weekly
Deworm every 6 months — available free for children
Prevent malaria — treated mosquito nets are highly effective
Space pregnancies — repeated pregnancies without recovery depletes iron stores
For children: ensure they eat varied diet with iron sources from 6 months

see_doctor_if: Severe breathlessness or chest pain with anaemia
Fainting or near-fainting episodes
Anaemia in pregnancy — any severity needs medical attention
Child who is very pale, listless, or breathless
Anaemia that does not improve with 3 months of iron supplements
anaemia.local_context: Anaemia is extremely common across Uganda, particularly in women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and young children. The Ugandan diet is often iron-poor — high in carbohydrate staples with limited meat and dark leafy vegetables. Free iron supplements and deworming tablets are available at all government health centres.
home_remedies: Leafy greens cooked in a cast iron pot — the iron from the pot actually transfers into food
Beans cooked with tomatoes — iron + vitamin C combination enhances absorption significantly
Liver once a week — extremely iron-dense, also provides B12 and folate
Silver fish (mukene) — abundant in Uganda, excellent iron and protein source
Avoid tea with meals — switch to water or juice instead to maximise iron absorption

depression.name: Depression
depression.description: A serious mental health condition characterised by persistent low mood, loss of interest, fatigue, and feelings of worthlessness lasting at least 2 weeks. Not simply 'feeling sad' — depression is a medical condition with clear biological causes and effective treatments. Nearly 1 in 3 Ugandans will experience a mental health condition in their lifetime.
depression.body_mechanism: Depression involves actual changes in brain chemistry — particularly serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine — and brain structure. Chronic stress causes the hippocampus (memory centre) to shrink. Inflammation markers increase. These are not character weaknesses — they are measurable biological changes. The brain in depression literally processes information differently, making negative thoughts feel overwhelmingly true and the future feel hopeless.
depression.epidemiology_uganda: A 2022 analysis found nearly 1 in 3 Ugandans (32%) experience a mental illness at some point. The 2024 National Household Survey found 5.5 million people facing probable mental health challenges. Uganda has fewer than 100 psychiatrists for 45 million people. Depression is dramatically under-diagnosed and under-treated.

immediate: You are not weak. Depression is a medical condition, not a character flaw or spiritual failure
Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling — isolation worsens depression
Get outside and move your body — even a 15-minute walk has measurable antidepressant effect
Maintain a basic routine — wake at the same time, eat regular meals, sleep at consistent time
If you are having thoughts of harming yourself: tell someone NOW and go to hospital or call for help
short_term: See a doctor or counsellor — depression responds very well to treatment
Antidepressant medication (if prescribed) takes 2-4 weeks to work — continue taking it
Exercise daily — has proven antidepressant effects comparable to medication in mild-moderate cases
Reduce or eliminate alcohol — it is a depressant that worsens symptoms even though it temporarily numbs pain
Maintain social contact even when you don't want to — isolation is depression's greatest ally
long_term: Counselling or talk therapy — highly effective when combined with medication
Build a reliable daily routine — structure is protective against depression
Regular physical activity — 30 minutes of aerobic exercise 5 days a week
Treat underlying causes: address financial stress, relationship problems, trauma
Faith community and social support — proven protective factors against relapse

see_doctor_if: ANY thoughts of suicide or self-harm — seek help immediately
Symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks that are affecting work, relationships, or daily function
Severe depression with inability to eat or get out of bed
Depression in a pregnant or postpartum woman — requires immediate specialist care
If medication does not seem to be working after 4 weeks — dosage may need adjustment
depression.local_context: Mental health challenges carry significant stigma in Uganda — many people attribute depression to spiritual causes, character weakness, or witchcraft. This delays treatment and causes enormous suffering. Depression is a medical condition with effective treatments. Butabika National Referral Hospital provides specialist care. Many district hospitals have counsellors. Faith leaders are increasingly being trained to recognise and refer mental health conditions.
home_remedies: Physical exercise — the single most evidence-based non-pharmacological antidepressant
Social connection — visit a friend, attend a community gathering, talk to family
Sunlight exposure — 20-30 minutes of morning sunlight has proven mood-lifting effects
Omega-3 rich foods: fish, especially mukene (silver fish) — associated with lower depression rates
Establish a sleep routine — poor sleep and depression reinforce each other dangerously

malaria_severe.name: Severe Malaria
malaria_severe.description: A life-threatening form of malaria where Plasmodium falciparum parasites (97% of Uganda malaria) overwhelm the body's defences and begin damaging the brain, kidneys, lungs, and blood clotting system. Most common in children under 5 and pregnant women. Causes tens of thousands of deaths in Uganda annually.
malaria_severe.body_mechanism: In severe malaria, infected red blood cells clump together and stick to blood vessel walls in the brain (cerebral malaria), lungs, and kidneys — blocking circulation. The brain starves for oxygen causing seizures and coma. Red blood cells rupture faster than the body can replace them causing severe anaemia. The immune response causes extreme inflammation throughout the body. Without IV treatment within hours, death or permanent brain damage results.

immediate: THIS IS AN EMERGENCY — GO TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait.
Give paracetamol to bring down the fever while transporting to hospital
If seizure occurs: lay patient on their side, clear airway, do not put anything in mouth
Do not give food or drink if unconscious — risk of aspiration
Call ahead to hospital if possible — they need to prepare IV artesunate
short_term: IV artesunate in hospital — the only effective treatment
Blood transfusion if severely anaemic
Seizure control medications
IV fluids under careful monitoring
long_term: Prevent future malaria — mosquito nets every night
Prompt treatment of any future fever
Malaria testing before any fever treatment

see_doctor_if: ANY malaria with confusion, seizures, or inability to respond — EMERGENCY
Child who cannot sit, stand, or respond normally with fever
Malaria with severe anaemia — pale gums and conjunctiva, extreme weakness
Malaria with breathing difficulty
Dark or black urine with malaria — indicates severe haemolysis
malaria_severe.local_context: Severe malaria kills thousands of children in Uganda each year — the northern and eastern regions have the highest burden. Every second counts. Government hospitals have IV artesunate which is the most effective treatment. Never treat severe malaria at home with oral medications. Transport to hospital immediately.
home_remedies: SEVERE MALARIA HAS NO EFFECTIVE HOME TREATMENT
Give paracetamol only to lower fever WHILE going to hospital
Keep patient cool and hydrated WHILE going to hospital
Hospital IV artesunate is the only life-saving treatment

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.description: A medical emergency where blood flow to part of the brain is suddenly cut off — either by a clot (ischaemic stroke, 80% of cases) or a burst blood vessel (haemorrhagic stroke). Every minute of stroke untreated, 1.9 million brain cells die. Stroke is the third leading cause of disability in Uganda.
stroke.body_mechanism: Brain cells are extremely sensitive to oxygen deprivation. When a blood vessel is blocked or ruptures, the area of brain it supplies starts dying within minutes. The FAST symptoms (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call for help) reflect which area of the brain is affected. The damage is permanent — only emergency treatment within hours can salvage the affected brain tissue.

immediate: USE THE FAST TEST: Face drooping? Arm weakness? Speech slurred? Time — go NOW
GO TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY — stroke treatment is time-critical, every minute matters
Note the exact time symptoms started — this determines treatment options
Do not give food, water, or medication by mouth — they may not be able to swallow
Lay the patient on their side if unconscious — prevents choking
short_term: Hospital emergency assessment and treatment
CT scan to determine stroke type
Clot-busting drugs if ischaemic and within 4.5 hours
Blood pressure control
long_term: Rehabilitation
Blood pressure medication
Antiplatelet drugs
Risk factor management

see_doctor_if: ANY of the FAST signs — Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty — GO NOW
Sudden severe headache described as the worst ever — possible haemorrhagic stroke
Sudden loss of vision in one eye
Sudden inability to walk or loss of coordination
stroke.local_context: Stroke risk in Uganda is rising rapidly due to increasing hypertension, diabetes, and lifestyle changes. High blood pressure is the single most important stroke risk factor — and most Ugandans with hypertension are untreated. Controlling blood pressure prevents stroke more effectively than any other single intervention.
home_remedies: STROKE IS AN EMERGENCY — no home remedies are appropriate
Get to hospital as fast as possible
PREVENTION: Control blood pressure. Take medication daily. Monitor regularly.
PREVENTION: Reduce salt, exercise daily, stop smoking, control diabetes

preeclampsia.name: Pre-eclampsia / Eclampsia
preeclampsia.description: A serious pregnancy complication characterised by high blood pressure and organ damage, typically after 20 weeks. Pre-eclampsia is the leading cause of maternal death in Uganda. Eclampsia (seizures with pre-eclampsia) is immediately life-threatening to both mother and baby.
preeclampsia.body_mechanism: The placenta releases substances that damage blood vessels throughout the body. Blood pressure rises dramatically, the kidneys spill protein into urine, and fluid accumulates in tissues (causing swelling). The brain becomes vulnerable to seizures (eclampsia). The liver and blood clotting system can also fail. Both mother and baby are at immediate risk without hospitalisation.

immediate: GO TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY — pre-eclampsia is a medical emergency
If seizure occurs: lay on left side, protect from injury, clear airway
Do not give herbal medicines or traditional remedies — they can worsen the condition
Record when symptoms started and what happened
Delivery is the only cure — the decision about timing is for doctors to make
short_term: Hospitalisation and monitoring
Blood pressure medication
Magnesium sulphate to prevent seizures
Monitoring of baby
long_term: Blood pressure monitoring post-delivery
Follow-up to check kidneys
Future pregnancy planning with doctor

see_doctor_if: ANY pregnant woman after 20 weeks with severe headache — go to hospital TODAY
Swollen face, hands, or feet in pregnancy — always needs assessment
Blurred vision or seeing flashing lights in pregnancy
Severe upper abdominal pain in pregnancy
Seizure in pregnancy — EMERGENCY, go immediately
preeclampsia.local_context: Pre-eclampsia is the leading direct cause of maternal death in Uganda. Many women die because they do not recognise the warning signs or delay seeking care. Every pregnant woman should know: if you develop severe headache, vision changes, or severe swelling after 6 months of pregnancy — go to hospital TODAY. Magnesium sulphate (the life-saving treatment) is available at all regional hospitals.
home_remedies: PRE-ECLAMPSIA HAS NO HOME TREATMENT — it is a medical emergency
Bed rest on the left side can reduce blood pressure temporarily WHILE going to hospital
Do not take herbal medicines — they can interact dangerously with medications
Prevention: attend all antenatal care appointments. Blood pressure is checked at each visit.

angina.name: Angina Pectoris (Chest Pain on Exertion)
angina.description: Chest pain or discomfort caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, typically triggered by physical activity or stress and relieved by rest. It is a warning sign of coronary artery disease.
angina.body_mechanism: The heart muscle needs a constant oxygen supply delivered by the coronary arteries. When these arteries are narrowed by plaque (atherosclerosis), extra demand during exertion cannot be met. The oxygen-starved muscle sends pain signals — felt as tightness, pressure, or squeezing in the chest, sometimes radiating to the left arm or jaw.

immediate: Stop all physical activity immediately — sit or lie down
If prescribed GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) spray or tablet: use it under your tongue now
Loosen any tight clothing around your chest
If pain does not improve within 5 minutes after rest or GTN, or if this is your first episode: go to hospital NOW — this may be a heart attack
Chew one aspirin (325mg) if available and you are not allergic — do NOT swallow whole
short_term: See a doctor urgently if this is a new symptom or is getting worse
Do not ignore worsening or more frequent angina — it can precede a heart attack
Keep a record of when pain occurs, how long it lasts, and what triggers it
long_term: Take all prescribed medications daily — especially aspirin, beta-blockers, and statins
Reduce salt, saturated fat, and fried food intake
Stop smoking completely — smoking is a major cause of coronary artery disease
Regular moderate exercise as guided by your doctor
Lose weight if overweight — even 5% weight loss reduces cardiac strain

see_doctor_if: Any chest pain that does not go away with 5 minutes of rest or GTN
Chest pain at rest — this is unstable angina, a medical emergency
Pain radiating to your left arm, jaw, neck, or back
New-onset chest pain of any kind
Chest pain with sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath
home_remedies: Rest immediately when pain begins
Deep slow breathing to reduce anxiety and lower heart rate
Avoid large heavy meals — they increase demand on the heart
Avoid extreme cold — cold constricts coronary arteries
angina.local_context: Angina is increasingly common in Uganda as diets shift toward more salt and fat, and physical activity declines in cities. It is often missed because chest pain is attributed to other causes. If you experience chest tightness on climbing stairs or walking uphill, please see a doctor.

acute_coronary_syndrome.name: Possible Heart Attack (Acute Coronary Syndrome)
acute_coronary_syndrome.description: A life-threatening emergency where blood supply to part of the heart is suddenly blocked. Without immediate treatment, heart muscle begins to die. Time is critical — every minute of delay causes more permanent damage.
acute_coronary_syndrome.body_mechanism: A plaque (fatty deposit) in a coronary artery ruptures, triggering an emergency clotting response. The clot blocks blood flow completely. The heart muscle supplied by that artery is starved of oxygen and begins to die — causing the characteristic crushing chest pain and life-threatening heart rhythm problems.

immediate: CALL FOR EMERGENCY HELP IMMEDIATELY — do not drive yourself to hospital
Chew 300–325mg aspirin NOW if available and not allergic (do not swallow whole — chew it)
Sit or lie in whatever position is most comfortable
Loosen all tight clothing
Stay as calm as possible — minimize physical effort
If you have GTN spray or sublingual tablet: use it
If unconscious with no pulse: begin CPR and call for help
short_term: Hospital treatment is the ONLY effective treatment — thrombolysis or angioplasty must happen within hours
Every 10-minute delay increases permanent heart muscle damage
long_term: Lifelong medication after a heart attack: aspirin, statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor
Cardiac rehabilitation programme
Stop smoking completely
Strict blood pressure and diabetes control
Regular cardiac follow-up

see_doctor_if: ANY crushing, squeezing, or heavy chest pain — especially if not relieved by rest
Chest pain with left arm pain, jaw pain, or back pain
Chest pain with sweating and nausea
Chest pain with shortness of breath
Any chest pain lasting more than 5 minutes that does not fully go away with rest
home_remedies: This is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY — there are no effective home remedies
Aspirin (chewed, not swallowed) is the only home intervention with proven benefit
Call for emergency transport to hospital immediately
acute_coronary_syndrome.local_context: Heart attacks are increasingly common in Uganda and are often fatal because patients delay going to hospital, hoping the pain will pass. Mulago National Referral Hospital and major regional hospitals have cardiac units. Do not wait — the difference between life and death in a heart attack is often measured in minutes.

gerd.name: GERD / Acid Reflux (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease)
gerd.description: A condition where stomach acid regularly flows back up into the oesophagus (food pipe), causing a burning sensation in the chest or throat. Very common and usually manageable with lifestyle changes and medication.
gerd.body_mechanism: The lower oesophageal sphincter — a ring of muscle at the top of the stomach — normally acts as a one-way valve. When it weakens or relaxes inappropriately, acidic stomach contents flow back up, irritating and burning the unprotected oesophageal lining, causing the characteristic burning pain that can be mistaken for chest pain.

immediate: Sit upright — lying down worsens acid reflux
Take an antacid if available (sodium bicarbonate in water, milk, or commercial antacid)
Sip cold water slowly — dilutes acid and may temporarily reduce burning
Avoid food, coffee, tea, or citrus until symptoms settle
short_term: Avoid large meals — eat smaller, more frequent portions
Wait 2–3 hours after eating before lying down
Avoid common triggers: spicy food, fried food, alcohol, coffee, tea, citrus, tomatoes
Elevate the head of your bed by 15–20cm if symptoms occur at night
Over-the-counter antacids (omeprazole, ranitidine) are widely available
long_term: Maintain healthy weight — excess abdominal weight increases abdominal pressure
Stop smoking — nicotine weakens the lower oesophageal sphincter
Avoid eating within 3 hours of sleep
See a doctor if symptoms occur more than twice a week — may need prescription medication

see_doctor_if: Difficulty swallowing food or liquids
Unintentional weight loss
Vomiting blood or black stool
Symptoms despite lifestyle changes and antacids
Symptoms more than 2 times per week for more than 3 weeks
home_remedies: Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) in water — neutralises stomach acid temporarily
Cold milk — provides temporary relief through acid neutralisation
Ginger tea — has anti-inflammatory properties
Aloe vera juice — may soothe the oesophagus
Chewing gum after meals — increases saliva production which neutralises acid
gerd.local_context: Acid reflux is very common in Uganda, often triggered by spicy foods, posho, and eating large late-night meals. Many people confuse the chest burning of acid reflux with heart problems. The key difference: acid reflux burning usually starts after meals and is associated with a sour/acidic taste in the mouth.

costochondritis.name: Costochondritis (Chest Wall Pain)
costochondritis.description: Inflammation of the cartilage connecting the ribs to the breastbone, causing chest pain that is often sharp and worsens with movement or pressing on the chest. It is not dangerous and not related to the heart.
costochondritis.body_mechanism: The costochondral junctions — where rib cartilage meets the breastbone — become inflamed, usually from minor trauma, vigorous coughing, or unknown causes. This inflammation causes localised chest pain that is reproducible by pressing the area, and worsens with deep breathing or certain movements.

immediate: Take ibuprofen or paracetamol as directed — these reduce inflammation and pain
Apply a warm compress to the painful area
Rest and avoid activities that worsen the pain
short_term: Anti-inflammatory medications (ibuprofen) for 1–2 weeks
Avoid activities that strain the chest wall: heavy lifting, vigorous exercise, lying in certain positions
Use heat therapy — warm cloth or hot water bottle on the chest wall
long_term: Most cases resolve within a few weeks without treatment
Avoid the triggering activity if identified
See a doctor if pain persists beyond 3–4 weeks

see_doctor_if: Chest pain is severe and not reproduced by pressing the chest
Associated with shortness of breath, arm pain, or sweating
Fever is present
Pain has persisted for more than a month without improvement
home_remedies: Warm compress on painful area — reduces muscle and cartilage inflammation
Ibuprofen from any pharmacy — most effective anti-inflammatory for this condition
Rest and avoid heavy lifting for 1–2 weeks
Gentle stretching of the chest — if tolerated
costochondritis.local_context: Costochondritis is a very common cause of chest pain in Uganda, especially in people who do heavy manual labour, carry heavy loads, or have been coughing severely. It is harmless but can be frightening because it feels like heart pain. The key test: if pressing on your chest with a finger reproduces or worsens the pain, it is almost certainly costochondritis, not a heart problem.

pleuritis.name: Pleuritis / Pleurisy (Inflamed Lung Lining)
pleuritis.description: Inflammation of the pleura — the two-layered membrane surrounding the lungs. Causes sharp chest pain that worsens dramatically with every breath, cough, or movement. Always requires investigation to find the underlying cause.
pleuritis.body_mechanism: The pleural membranes normally slide smoothly over each other during breathing. When inflamed, their surfaces become rough and rub against each other like sandpaper with every breath, causing sharp, stabbing pain. The inflammation may be caused by infection, autoimmune disease, or fluid accumulation.

immediate: Take a pain reliever — ibuprofen works best as it reduces inflammation
Lie on the side of the pain — this may reduce the pain slightly
Breathe shallowly if deep breathing is very painful
If severely breathless or in extreme pain: go to hospital
short_term: See a doctor — pleuritis always needs investigation to find the cause
The underlying cause (infection, TB, etc.) needs specific treatment
Do not ignore this — TB is a common cause in Uganda
long_term: Treatment depends on the cause
TB-related pleuritis: full 6-month TB treatment
Viral pleuritis: usually resolves in 1–2 weeks

see_doctor_if: Sharp chest pain that worsens with every breath
Difficulty breathing
Fever with chest pain
Any chest pain of this type — it requires diagnosis to rule out TB, pneumonia, and other serious causes
home_remedies: Ibuprofen — most effective pain relief for pleuritis
Rest in a comfortable position
Apply warm compress to chest — may reduce discomfort
pleuritis.local_context: In Uganda, pleuritis is often caused by tuberculosis or pneumonia. Sharp chest pain that gets worse when you breathe deeply should always be seen by a health worker — TB is very treatable when caught early, and is FREE to treat at government facilities.

fu_diabetes_thirst.question: Are you feeling extremely thirsty — drinking far more water than usual — and needing to urinate much more frequently, even at night?

fu_diabetes_fatigue.question: Is your fatigue persistent — meaning you feel tired even after sleeping — and are you losing weight without trying to?

fu_diabetes_family.question: Does diabetes run in your family — parent, sibling, or close relative with diabetes?

fu_diabetes_weight.question: Are you overweight, or have you gained significant weight in the past few years?

fu_tb_cough_duration.question: How long have you been coughing? Has it been more than 2 weeks?

fu_tb_night_sweats.question: Are you waking up at night drenched in sweat — soaking your clothes or bedding?

fu_tb_blood.question: Have you ever coughed up blood, or have you noticed blood in your mucus?

fu_tb_contact.question: Have you been in close contact with someone who has tuberculosis (TB), or who has a chronic cough?

fu_tb_hiv.question: Do you know your HIV status? Being HIV positive significantly changes the urgency of evaluating a cough.

fu_pneumonia_breathing.question: Is your breathing unusually fast or laboured — are you having to work hard to breathe?

fu_pneumonia_lips.question: Are your lips or fingertips turning blue or very pale?

fu_pneumonia_confusion.question: Are you feeling confused, or is it hard to stay awake and follow a conversation?

fu_sickle_known.question: Have you been told you have sickle cell disease, or have you ever had a sickle cell test?

fu_sickle_pain_location.question: Where is the pain — in your bones, joints, chest, or abdomen?

fu_sickle_trigger.question: Did anything trigger this episode — cold weather, dehydration, illness, or intense physical activity?

fu_nutrition_diet.question: How would you describe your usual diet — do you eat a variety of foods including protein, vegetables, and fruits regularly?

fu_nutrition_child.question: Is this for a child — and if so, how old are they and how long have they had these symptoms?

fu_nutrition_pregnancy.question: Are you currently pregnant or have you recently given birth?

fu_eye_discharge.question: What kind of discharge does the eye have — thick yellow or green pus, watery discharge, or no discharge?

fu_eye_both.question: Is it affecting one eye or both eyes?

fu_eye_vision.question: Is your vision affected — is it blurred or reduced?

fu_diarrhoea_blood.question: Is there blood or mucus in the diarrhoea?

fu_diarrhoea_duration.question: How long have you had diarrhoea — and how many loose stools per day?

fu_diarrhoea_child.question: Is this for a child, especially under 5 years old?

fu_anaemia_diet.question: How often do you eat iron-rich foods — meat, liver, beans, or dark leafy greens?

fu_anaemia_bleeding.question: Have you had any unusual bleeding — heavy periods, blood in stool, or frequent nosebleeds?

fu_anaemia_pregnancy.question: Are you pregnant or have you recently given birth?

fu_depression_duration.question: How long have you been feeling this way — more than 2 weeks?

fu_depression_function.question: Is this affecting your ability to work, study, or take care of daily responsibilities?

fu_depression_safety.question: Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to be alive?

fu_depression_sleep.question: How is your sleep — are you sleeping too much, too little, or waking very early?

fu_water_source.question: What is your main source of drinking water — piped water, borehole, well, or river?

fu_malaria_test.question: Have you been tested for malaria recently — either a rapid test or blood smear?

fu_typhoid_test.question: Have you had a blood test or Widal test for typhoid?

fu_painkiller_use.question: Do you take ibuprofen, aspirin, or diclofenac regularly — for pain, malaria, or other conditions?

fu_respiratory.question: Do you have a cough, and is your breathing faster or more difficult than usual?

fu_worse_at_night.question: Are your breathing symptoms worse at night or early morning — do you wake up coughing or wheezing?

fu_triggers.question: Do you notice your breathing problems are triggered by anything specific — dust, smoke, cold air, exercise, or animals?

fu_family_history_htn.question: Does hypertension (high blood pressure) or stroke run in your family?

fu_headache_location.question: Where is the headache — at the back of your head, the top, or all over?

fu_chest_exertion.question: Does the chest pain happen mainly when you are physically active — walking, climbing stairs, lifting things — and go away when you rest?

fu_chest_relief.question: Does the chest pain go away completely when you stop the activity and rest for a few minutes?

fu_chest_radiation.question: Does the chest pain spread (radiate) to any other part of your body — like your left arm, shoulder, jaw, neck, or back?

fu_chest_duration.question: How long does the chest pain last when it occurs?

fu_acs_onset.question: Did the chest pain come on suddenly, or has it been building gradually?

fu_acs_quality.question: How would you best describe the chest pain — crushing or squeezing, sharp and stabbing, burning, or aching/pressure?

fu_acs_radiation.question: Is the pain spreading to your left arm, jaw, neck, or back?

fu_acs_associated.question: Along with the chest pain, are you also experiencing sweating, nausea, or feeling faint?

fu_acs_risk.question: Do you have any of these risk factors: high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking history, or family members with heart attacks?

fu_acid_timing.question: Does the burning chest feeling mainly occur after meals, when lying down, or at night?

fu_acid_food.question: Is the burning feeling triggered or worsened by spicy food, fried food, coffee, or acidic drinks?

fu_acid_position.question: Do you notice a sour or bitter taste in your mouth, especially when you bend over or lie down?

fu_acid_severity.question: Has this been happening more than twice a week for the past few weeks?

fu_chest_touch.question: If you press firmly with your finger on the painful area of your chest, does it reproduce or significantly worsen the pain?

fu_chest_movement.question: Does the chest pain clearly get worse when you twist your body, raise your arms above your head, or take a very deep breath?

fu_chest_location.question: Can you point to exactly where the chest pain is — is it on one side of the chest, near the breastbone (centre), or is it a general, diffuse pain you cannot pinpoint?

fu_pleurisy_breathing.question: Does the chest pain get dramatically sharper when you take a deep breath in?

fu_pleurisy_cause.question: Have you recently had a respiratory illness — cough, flu, or any illness involving breathing difficulties?

emergency_flags.name: Mental Health Crisis
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ IMPORTANT: You mentioned thoughts of harming yourself. Please know that you are not alone and help is available. Please tell someone you trust right now, or go to Butabika National Referral Hospital (Kampala) or your nearest health facility. You matter and this can get better.

emergency_flags.name: Severe Malaria — Child
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: A child with high fever and altered consciousness in Uganda must be treated as severe malaria until proven otherwise. This is a medical emergency. Go to hospital IMMEDIATELY. Every minute matters.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Diabetic Emergency
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: If this person has diabetes and is confused or semi-conscious, this could be a diabetic emergency (hypoglycaemia or DKA). If they can swallow safely, give sugar immediately. If not — go to hospital NOW.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Pre-eclampsia
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: Severe headache or swelling during pregnancy can be pre-eclampsia — a life-threatening emergency for mother and baby. Go to the nearest hospital or health centre immediately. Do not wait.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Sepsis
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ EMERGENCY: High fever with confusion and breathing difficulty could indicate sepsis — a life-threatening response to infection. Go to hospital immediately. This condition deteriorates rapidly.

emergency_flags.name: Possible Heart Attack
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: Chest pain spreading to your arm or jaw can be a sign of a heart attack — a life-threatening emergency. **Please call for help immediately or go to the nearest hospital NOW. Do not drive yourself. Chew an aspirin if you have one.**

emergency_flags.name: Severe Chest Pain — Needs Urgent Assessment
emergency_flags.message: ⚠️ URGENT: Severe chest pain that does not go away with rest needs urgent medical assessment. Please go to a hospital or clinic as soon as possible. This may be a heart problem, and early treatment saves lives.
